message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"5.16","text":"Therefore, dearest, I have set before you, one by one, the love affairs of all the more notable gods, so that you may know that jealousy about this arises among foolish human beings alone. That is why they happen to be mortal and pass their lives miserably: because, through their own jealousy, they have declared to be evil what the gods regarded as good. From now on, then, you will be blessed if you imitate gods and not human beings. For when human beings see you preserving what is regarded as chastity, they praise you because of their own passion, but they do not benefit you; the gods, however, when they see you making yourself like them, will both praise you and benefit you.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἐκ μέρους","chosen":"one by one","rationale":"In this cataloguing context the phrase indicates presentation by individual instances; “in part” is also lexically possible but less suitable here."},{"source_quote":"περὶ τούτου γίνεται ζηλοτυπία","chosen":"jealousy about this arises","rationale":"ζηλοτυπία denotes sexual or possessive jealousy, while γίνεται presents it as arising or occurring."},{"source_quote":"τὴν νομιζομένην σωφροσύνην","chosen":"what is regarded as chastity","rationale":"σωφροσύνη here concerns sexual restraint, while νομιζομένην marks it as conventionally regarded rather than endorsing it as genuine."},{"source_quote":"ἐξομοιουμένην σε ἑαυτοῖς","chosen":"you making yourself like them","rationale":"The participle describes assimilation to the gods, not merely outward imitation."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"5.17","text":"Consider, then, how many beloved women they rewarded: some of them they made into stars, while they also bestowed benefits on the children and helpers of some. For example, Zeus made Callisto into a star—the so-called Little Bear, which some also call the Dog’s Tail. Because of Amphitrite, Poseidon assigned the Dolphin a place in heaven; and because of Euryale, his mother, he judged Orion, the son of Euryale daughter of Minos, worthy of the stars. Dionysus did the same with Ariadne’s crown. Zeus gave the Eagle, which had assisted in the abduction of Ganymede, its appointed place, assigned Ganymede himself the honor of Aquarius, and honored the Bull because of Europa. To please Leda, he also made Castor, Polydeuces, and Helen into stars; likewise Perseus because of Danae, Arcas because of Callisto, the Maiden—also called Dike—because of Themis, and Heracles because of Alcmene. I will not prolong this any further. It would take a long time to recount individually how many others the gods have benefited because of their many beloved women, through their unions with human beings—unions that foolish people prohibit as evil practices, not knowing that pleasure is the great enjoyment among human beings.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"πόσας ἠμείψαντο ἐρωμένας","chosen":"how many beloved women they rewarded","rationale":"ἀμείβομαι here has the favorable sense “reward,” and ἐρωμένας denotes women who were objects of erotic love."},{"source_quote":"τὴν λεγομένην ἄρκτον μικράν","chosen":"the so-called Little Bear","rationale":"The translation preserves μικράν even though Callisto is more commonly associated with the Great Bear in other traditions."},{"source_quote":"Δελφῖνα","chosen":"the Dolphin","rationale":"The constellation-associated figure is rendered by the transparent English animal name rather than treated as an otherwise unattested personal name."},{"source_quote":"Διόνυσος τὸν Ἀριάδνης στέφανον","chosen":"Dionysus did the same with Ariadne’s crown","rationale":"The Greek is a verbless catalog entry; the action of placing or honoring among the stars is supplied from the immediately surrounding entries without specifying more than the context supports."},{"source_quote":"ἐν Ὑδροχόου τιμῇ ἔταξεν","chosen":"assigned Ganymede himself the honor of Aquarius","rationale":"τιμή can denote an honor, rank, or honored station; here it identifies Ganymede’s celestial role as Aquarius."},{"source_quote":"παρθένον τὴν καὶ Δίκην","chosen":"the Maiden—also called Dike","rationale":"The article-plus-καί construction introduces Dike as an additional designation for the Maiden."},{"source_quote":"ταῖς πρὸς ἀνθρώπους κοινωνίαις","chosen":"through their unions with human beings","rationale":"κοινωνία can mean association or participation; the erotic context supports “unions,” while the dative expresses the means or setting of the benefits."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"Γανυμήδους.ἁρπαγῇ","issue":"The printed full stop interrupts the single phrase “the abduction of Ganymede.” It is treated as intrusive punctuation, not as a sentence boundary; the selected edition’s wording is otherwise retained.","proposed_reading":"Γανυμήδους ἁρπαγῇ","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"καὶ.Δίκην","issue":"The printed full stop separates καί from the coordinated name it introduces. The syntax remains clear, and the translation treats the punctuation as intrusive.","proposed_reading":"καὶ Δίκην","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"5.18","text":"And what of this? Do not the renowned among the wise also prefer pleasure and have intercourse with whatever women they wished? First among them is the teacher of Greece, about whom Phoebus himself said, “Of all men, Socrates is wisest”: does he not propose women in common in Lacedaemon, the city with the best laws, and cover handsome Alcibiades beneath his threadbare cloak? And does not the Socratic Antisthenes write that what is called adultery must not be rejected? Did not his student Diogenes openly have intercourse with Lais in public, at the price of carrying her on his shoulders? Does not Epicurus prefer pleasure? Does not Aristippus, after perfuming himself, give his whole self to Aphrodite? Does not Zeno, hinting that such matters are indifferent, say that the divine exists throughout everything, so that it may become clear to the discerning—namely, that whoever one has intercourse with, one has intercourse as with oneself, and that it is superfluous to prohibit so-called adulteries or unions with a mother, daughter, sister, or children? And in his erotic letters Chrysippus even mentions the image at Argos, placing Hera’s face close to Zeus’s genitals.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"κοινὰς προτίθησι τὰς γυναῖκας","chosen":"propose women in common","rationale":"The phrase describes advocating that women be held or shared in common; the compact English preserves the source’s philosophical formulation."},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ τῷ τρίβωνι","chosen":"beneath his threadbare cloak","rationale":"τρίβων denotes the worn cloak conventionally associated with philosophers."},{"source_quote":"Λαΐδι οὐκ ἐπὶ μισθῷ τοῦ φέρειν αὐτὴν ἐπ’ ὤμων δημοσίᾳ κοινωνεῖ","chosen":"Did not … openly have intercourse with Lais in public, at the price of carrying her on his shoulders?","rationale":"οὐκ supplies the expected negative form of the rhetorical question, while ἐπὶ μισθῷ identifies the carrying as the price or condition of the intercourse."},{"source_quote":"ἀδιαφορεῖν αἰνισσόμενος","chosen":"hinting that such matters are indifferent","rationale":"ἀδιαφορεῖν invokes the philosophical category of things lacking moral differentiation, and αἰνισσόμενος indicates an indirect or enigmatic suggestion."},{"source_quote":"διὰ πάντων τὸ θεῖον εἶναι","chosen":"the divine exists throughout everything","rationale":"διὰ πάντων can mean “through all things” or “throughout everything”; the latter gives readable English without turning τὸ θεῖον into a personal deity not explicitly named."},{"source_quote":"παίδων","chosen":"children","rationale":"The word can denote children, offspring, or boys. “Children” best fits the surrounding kinship list, while “boys” remains a possible alternative."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τῷ τοῦ Διὸς αἰδοίῳ φέρων τῆς Ἥρας τὸ πρόσωπον","chosen":"placing Hera’s face close to Zeus’s genitals","rationale":"πρός with the dative expresses proximity, and φέρων portrays Chrysippus’s description or presentation of the image."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἵνα γνώριμον τοῖς συνετοῖς γένηται ἵνα ᾧ ἂν τις μιγῇ","issue":"The repeated ἵνα produces an awkward construction. The translation takes the second occurrence as resumptive or epexegetic, introducing what is to become clear; no omission or textual correction is required for a defensible sense.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"5.19","text":"I know that these things appear frightening and utterly shameful to those uninitiated into the truth, but not to the gods and philosophers of the Greeks, nor to the mysteries of Dionysus and Demeter. But above all these things—so that I do not waste my time recounting the lives of every god and philosopher—let your two greatest models be Zeus among the gods and Socrates among human philosophers. As for the rest, understand it from what I have written to remind you, and take care that you never grieve a lover of yours. For by acting contrary to gods and to those who are in love, you will be judged impious and undergo the fitting punishment. But if you offer yourself to every lover, you will receive benefit from the gods as one who imitates them. As for the rest, dearest, remember the mysteries I disclosed to you, and show me your decision by letter. Farewell.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τοῖς ἀληθείας ἀμυήτοις","chosen":"those uninitiated into the truth","rationale":"ἀμύητος uses the language of exclusion from initiation, anticipating the explicit reference to mysteries later in the sentence."},{"source_quote":"δύο ἔστωσάν σοι μέγιστοι σκοποί","chosen":"let your two greatest models be","rationale":"σκοποί literally denotes objects of attention or aims; here Zeus and Socrates function as exemplary standards to keep in view."},{"source_quote":"συνεῖσα ἔπεχε","chosen":"understand it … and take care","rationale":"The feminine imperatives direct the recipient first to comprehend the reminder and then to be on guard concerning the following prohibition."},{"source_quote":"παντὶ ἐραστῇ ἑαυτὴν παράσχῃς","chosen":"you offer yourself to every lover","rationale":"παρέχω with the reflexive means making oneself available or presenting oneself, and the erotic context is retained without euphemistic expansion."},{"source_quote":"περὶ ὧν σοι ἐξέφηνα μυστηρίων","chosen":"the mysteries I disclosed to you","rationale":"The relative construction is rendered idiomatically while preserving ἐξέφηνα as an explicit disclosure or revelation."},{"source_quote":"ἔρρωσό μοι","chosen":"Farewell","rationale":"The imperative literally wishes continued strength or health and functions as the conventional closing of a letter; the ethical dative μοι does not require a separate English object."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἐπεὶ ὡς θεοῖς καὶ ἐρῶσιν τὰ ἐναντία πράξασα","issue":"The function and attachment of ὡς before the coordinated datives are compressed and uncertain. The translation takes θεοῖς καὶ ἐρῶσιν with τὰ ἐναντία πράξασα, “acting contrary to gods and those who are in love.” An alternative is to understand the two datives as describing the same group, “the gods as themselves being lovers.”","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"5.20","text":"So I took this document from Appion as though I really intended to send it on to the beloved woman, but I made up a reply as though she had written back in answer to these things. When he came the next day, I delivered to Appion what was supposedly her reply. It read as follows:","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸ βιβλίον τοῦτο","chosen":"this document","rationale":"βιβλίον can denote a book, written document, or letter; the immediate context concerns a written communication to which a reply is fabricated."},{"source_quote":"ὡς ὄντως διαπέμψων αὐτὸ","chosen":"as though I really intended to send it on","rationale":"ὡς frames the future participle as a pretense, while ὄντως emphasizes the supposed genuineness of the intention."},{"source_quote":"ἐπλασάμην ὡς ἐκείνης πρὸς ταῦτα ἀντιγραψάσης","chosen":"I made up a reply as though she had written back in answer to these things","rationale":"πλάσσομαι denotes fabricating or inventing, and ἀντιγράφω here means writing a response."},{"source_quote":"ὡς δῆθεν τὴν παρ’ ἐκείνης ἀντιγραφήν","chosen":"what was supposedly her reply","rationale":"δῆθεν marks the reply as merely alleged or pretended, and παρ’ ἐκείνης identifies her as its purported source."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
